en: Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"Monks, if while you have gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty dwelling, there should arise in you fear, or trepidation, or horripilation,
then at that time you should recollect me by way of my physical form:

'Indeed, that Blessed One is a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans.'"
The Buddha, the Blessed One, should at that time recollect me in its various aspects. Whatever fear, trepidation, or horripilation may arise will be abandoned.
Monks, in the past, when a battle between the gods and the asuras was imminent, Śakra, the lord of the gods, addressed the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
"Friends, if while you have mounted [your chariots] for battle between the gods and the asuras, fear, trepidation, or horripilation should arise within you,

at that time you must call to mind my Vaijayanta banner-top. For those of you who, at that time, call to mind my Vaijayanta banner-top, whatever fear, trepidation, or horripilation may arise shall cease."

Or that bristling of the hair will be abandoned. Monks, it may happen that while you have gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty dwelling, fear, trepidation, or a bristling of the hair arises. At that time, you should recollect me by way of my physical form, thinking: "Thus indeed was he, the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Awakened One."
"Ānanda, for those who at that time recollect me from every aspect, whatever fear, trepidation, or horripilation may arise will be abandoned.

Why is that? Because Śakra, the lord of the gods, is still possessed of lust, hatred, and delusion; he is not yet liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair.
I say that he is not yet liberated from suffering."

The fearful, the trembling, the terrified, and the fleeing one— such a person fears even in solitude, trembles, and even flees. But I, indeed, have appeared in the world as a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the worlds, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.

Free from passion, free from hatred, free from delusion, liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair—liberated from suffering, I say. O monks, for me who am fearless, undaunted, unafraid, and not fleeing, my word is to be heard, my instruction is to be followed, and this matter is to be carried out. I am one who is fearless, undaunted, unafraid, and not fleeing. "This is the proper course," I declare.
Thus spoke the Blessed One. With joyful minds, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. The Dhvajāgra-sūtra is completed.
